machatzit_hashekel.en:
(Seif katan 11) A rope, etc. Although Rashi appears to imply, etc., nevertheless it seems to me that this is a scribal error, etc. The Rosh writes in the first chapter of Moed Katan 8a, on the Mishnah that burial chambers and graves may not be dug on Chol HaMoed, that Rashi explains this as referring to graves for people who have not yet died, to be used after the festival, and it is forbidden because of excessive exertion. The general rule that even on the second day of Yom Tov Jews may attend to a corpse applies only to moving it or another matter involving no significant exertion, such as washing it or cutting its hair, but not digging. Rashi's words are difficult: he initially explained that the graves are for people who will die later, so why cite the law that Jews may attend to a corpse on the second day of Yom Tov, which concerns burial that same day? Moreover, his statement “but not digging” implies that one may not dig a grave on the second day, which is incorrect, for the second day was treated as a weekday. The Rosh explains that Rashi was troubled by the following comparison. If a person dies late on the second day of Yom Tov and there is insufficient time to bury him that day, Jews may nevertheless attend to him that day for burial after Yom Tov. Why, then, should one not similarly dig graves on Chol HaMoed for burial after the festival? Rashi answers that only moving and acts without significant exertion were permitted in such a case, but not digging, since there is no time to bury him that day. Similarly, one may not cut his shroud, and the same applies on Chol HaMoed. We learn from this that if one dies on the second day and they do not intend to bury him that day, no prohibited melachah may be performed for him that day, apparently not even through a non-Jew. Terumas HaDeshen, siman 82, infers from the Rosh's mention only of moving that even carrying into a karmelis is forbidden. He then distinguishes between an actual melachah, namely carrying, and cutting hair, which he does not consider a melachah. Maharshal disagrees, maintaining that cutting hair is more of a melachah than carrying into a karmelis. Rather, the distinction is between laborious and non-laborious acts. A burdensome melachah is forbidden when burial will not take place that day, whereas cutting hair, although a Torah melachah, involves little exertion and is permitted. Certainly carrying into a karmelis would also be permitted according to the Rosh. Maharshal then writes that the text is nevertheless erroneous and disagrees with the Rosh. He argues that Rashi's question cannot have been based on the rule that the second day is like a weekday even when burial that day is impossible, because perhaps Jews may not attend to the corpse at all in such a case. Indeed, Rashi's own conclusion, allowing even the cutting of a shroud and myrtle, plainly refers only to a case in which they intend and have time to bury him that day. The opening statement that the second day was treated as a weekday must likewise refer only to burial that day. Therefore the text must be corrected. The Mishnah's opening may refer either to graves for those who will die later, or to graves for those who have already died. Rashi's question applies only to the second interpretation. According to the first interpretation, which is the accepted halachah, there is no question. Consequently, neither interpretation proves that any act, whether cutting hair or carrying, is permitted when burial is not intended that day. Regarding moving, see siman 311, where he discusses this at length.
See seif 8 and Magen Avraham there, seif katan 17.
It appears to me that what he wrote, etc. He sought to answer Maharshal's objections to Terumas HaDeshen, who wrote, as explained above, that cutting hair is not considered a melachah.
This is because he does not need the hair, etc. Eliyah Rabbah and Chemed Moshe understood Magen Avraham to mean that because he does not need the hair, it is a melachah not needed for its own purpose.
The Tur in siman 278 rules like Rabbi Shimon, that one is exempt for a melachah not needed for its own purpose. They therefore questioned Magen Avraham's conclusion that Rambam discusses one who needs the hair, meaning that Rambam rules like Rabbi Yehudah, who holds one liable for a melachah not needed for its own purpose, as Magen Avraham writes at the end of siman 334. In my humble opinion, this is not his meaning. If so, why did he mention a melachah not needed for its own purpose only regarding carrying and not regarding cutting hair? Moreover, he concludes that carrying still bears the name of a melachah, whereas here there is no melachah at all. He would also have had to say that Terumas HaDeshen disagrees with Rivash, cited by Magen Avraham in siman 303, seif katan 22, who holds that one is liable for cutting hair even when he does not need the hair, because that was how the melachah was performed in the Mishkan. Rather, Magen Avraham means that cutting hair from a corpse is not a melachah at all, even according to Rabbi Yehudah, who holds one liable for a melachah not needed for its own purpose. His reason is as he writes later: one who circumcises an eight-month infant on Shabbos has done nothing, etc. Although cutting skin or flesh from a living person incurs liability for detaching, as Taz writes at the end of siman 336, nevertheless an eight-month infant is considered dead, and cutting his flesh is like cutting ordinary flesh and involves no prohibition. What difference is there between circumcising and cutting the skin, or cutting hair? It follows that there is no prohibition of shearing or detaching from a corpse. The Yerushalmi and Rambam, who hold one liable even for cutting from a corpse because of shearing, refer to one who needs the hair, for then he assigns significance to the act as a melachah. A similar principle is cited by Magen Avraham in siman 318, seif katan 36, in the name of Maggid Mishneh: when one does not intend the act, it is inappropriate to call it an inevitable consequence and impose liability merely because, when intentional, it constitutes a melachah. When unintentional, there is no melachah at all, since he does not seek to fashion a utensil. This resembles cutting a twig, where one is exempt unless he cuts it to use as a toothpick. Whenever the liability is because of fashioning a utensil, one who does not fashion it is exempt, even according to Rabbi Yehudah, who generally holds one liable for an unintended act. See there.
Although carrying is also a melachah not needed for its own purpose. Meaning, according to our ruling that one is exempt for such a melachah and only a shevus remains, it was nevertheless not permitted, because it still bears the name of a melachah.
Nevertheless, etc. This is likewise implied, etc., by Shulchan Aruch, which mentions permission only to move the corpse and no other act.

machatzit_hashekel.he: (ס"ק יב) מותר כו' כמו בחליצה. ביבמות דף ק"ו ע"ב והכי קי"ל באה"ע סי' קס"ט סעיף נ' אם יבמה נפלה לפני יבם שאינו הגון לה. והוא אינו רוצה לחלוץ אלא א"כ תתן לו מאתים מטעין לו וא"ל שתתן לו אחר החליצה מאתים ובאמת אחר החליצה א"צ ליתן לו כלום. וכן עושים כאן דלצורך מצוה מותר. וכתב הרב"י שם הטעם דרש"י כ' הטעם דשכר שבת אסור משום דהוי כעין מקח וממכר. והא מקח וממכר גופה אין אסורה כ"א מדרבנן והוי שכר שבת כעין גזרה לגזרה. וע"כ הא דאסור שכר שבת אינו אלא חומרא בעלמא. לכן במקום מצוה מותר אלא שהט"ז כתב לקמן סי' תקפ"ה הלא המתירים לדבר מצוה צריכים ליישב דעת האוסרים מדתני' השוכראת הפועל לשמור פרה אדומה או זרעים לצורך העומר אין נותנים לו שכר שבת אף על גב דהוי לצורך מצוה. ולכן מסיק דלא הותר אפי' לדעת המתירים לצורך מצוה דוקא מצוה שהוא חובת היום כגון תקיעת שופר בר"ה וצ"ל דה"ה הכא דהמת מוטל לפניו ועליו לקברו היום שלא לעבור על לא תלין הוי מצוה שהיא חובת היום:
machatzit_hashekel.en: (Seif katan 12) It is permitted, etc. As in the law of chalitzah. Yevamos 106b, and so we rule in Even HaEzer 169:50: if a yevamah falls before a yavam who is unsuitable for her and he refuses to perform chalitzah unless she gives him two hundred zuz, he may be deceived by promising payment after the chalitzah, and afterward she need not pay him anything. The same is done here, and it is permitted for the sake of a mitzvah. Beit Yosef explains there that Rashi gives the reason that Shabbos wages are forbidden because they resemble commerce. Commerce itself is prohibited only D'Rabbanan, so Shabbos wages resemble a decree upon a decree. The prohibition is therefore only an added stringency, and was permitted for a mitzvah. Taz, however, writes below in siman 585 that those who permit payment for a mitzvah must reconcile the opposing view with the baraisa stating that one who hires a worker to guard the red heifer or grain for the Omer may not pay him for Shabbos, although this is for a mitzvah. He therefore concludes that even according to the permissive opinion, it is allowed only for a mitzvah that is an obligation of that day, such as shofar blowing on Rosh Hashanah. The same must apply here: the deceased lies before him and must be buried that day so as not to violate the prohibition against leaving a corpse overnight, and it is therefore a mitzvah that is the obligation of the day.

magen_avraham.he: קודם תפלה. כדי שיוכלו האוננים להתפלל ובזמנינו שעושין הכל ע"י עכו"ם אין לקוברן עד אחר אכילה (מ"ב סוף הספר) משמע דעתו כיון שקוברין ע"י עכו"ם מותרין האוננים להתפלל וצ"ע דהא אית' סי' ע"א דפטורין מתפלה ואפשר דס"ל כיון שאין רוצים לקברו עד אחר אכילה חייבים להתפלל כמו בלילה כמ"ש סי' תקמ"ח וביש"ש כ' ראיתי נוהג שקוברים קודם אכילה ואף על פי שכ' הכל בו קודם תפילה במדינתינו א"א להקדים כ"כ ומ"ש לקברו אחר אכיל' ל"נ דאי משום שמחת י"ט קאמרי הא ליתא דאם מת מצוה קודם למגילה ק"ו לשמחת י"ט ובזמנינו הכל נקר' מ"מ ועוד דאיתא במדרש דאסור לאכול סעודת קבע קודם שנקבר המת ולכן אם הוא אדם חשוב קוברים אותו מיד אחר יציאת בה"כ ואם לאו מקבצים מנין וקוברין אותו בשעה שהש"ץ אומר פיוטים עכ"ל ועכשיו נוהגים לקוברו בשחרית וע"פ הרוב נמשך בשעת התפלה ויש ליזהר בזה עסי' ע"ב ס"ב ונ"ל דאם הוא אדם חשוב שצריכים רבים ללוותו יוציאהו לבה"ק אחר יציאת בה"כ ויאכלו ואח"כ יקברוהו כראוי כמ"ש סי' תמ"ג ועמ"ש סי' תקמ"ז:
magen_avraham.en: Before prayer. In order that the onenim will be able to pray. In our times, when everything is done through non-Jews, they should not bury them until after eating, as in Mateh Binyamin at the end of the book. It implies that his view is that since they bury through non-Jews, the onenim are permitted to pray. This requires study, for it is stated in siman 71 that they are exempt from prayer. Perhaps he holds that since they do not want to bury him until after eating, they are obligated to pray, as at night, as written in siman 548. In Yam Shel Shlomo he wrote: I have seen the practice that they bury before eating. Although Kol Bo wrote before prayer, in our country it is impossible to do so early. But what they wrote, to bury him after eating, does not seem correct to me. If they say this because of the joy of Yom Tov, this is not so, for if a meis mitzvah precedes reading the Megillah, all the more so does he precede the joy of Yom Tov. In our times everyone is considered a meis mitzvah. Furthermore, it is stated in the Midrash that it is forbidden to eat a fixed meal before the dead is buried. Therefore, if he is an important person, they bury him immediately after leaving the synagogue; and if not, they gather a minyan and bury him while the shaliach tzibbur is saying piyyutim, end quote. Nowadays the practice is to bury him in the morning, and for the most part it extends into the time of prayer, and one must be careful about this; see siman 72, seif 2. It seems to me that if he is an important person whom many people must escort, they should take him out to the cemetery after leaving the synagogue, eat, and afterward bury him properly, as written in siman 443. See what I wrote in siman 547.

mishnah_berurah.he:
{נא} כשמת בליל יום טוב וכו' - וביו"ט ראשון שהוא על ידי עממין אפילו מת בלילה קוברין אחר האכילה או אחר התפלה וכ"ז למחבר דיו"ט ב' הוא ע"י ישראל אמנם לדידן דנוהגין אפילו ביו"ט ב' ע"י עממין א"כ יו"ט ראשון ושני שוין:
{נב} אחר האכילה - ויש שכתבו דמוטב לקברו בשעה שאומרים פיוטים ויזמינו עשרה בני אדם עכ"פ לקבורתו ואם הוא אדם חשוב שחייבים כולם ללוותו יוציאוהו לאחר התפלה וילווהו עד ביה"ק ויניחוהו שם וילכו לאכול ואח"כ יקברוהו ומ"מ אם הכל מוכן דהיינו הקבר והתכריכין ואפשר לקוברו קודם אכילה בענין שלא ימנעו עי"ז משמחת יו"ט עדיף טפי לקוברו קודם אכילה דבמדרש סמכו על קרא דלא תאכלו על הדם שאסור לאכול סעודה קבוע קודם שנקבר המת:
mishnah_berurah.en:
(1) {Na} When he died on the night of Yom Tov, etc. - and in the first Yot, which is by Ammin, he even died at night, after eating or after prayer, etc., per the author of Yom Tov 2, he is by Yisrael, indeed, to a friend, even in Yot 2, by Ammin, per the first and second Yot:

(ב) He said, “And it is a man who has written, that he should be buried, and that he shall be given to him, and that he shall be blessed, and if he is an important man who must all accompany him, he shall be brought to him, and he shall be blessed with him, and he shall not eat, nor shall he be eaten, and shall he be able to eat from the grave, and that he shall not be able to eat A:

turei_zahav.he: קוברין אותו אחר אכילה. רש"ל כ' ע"ז ול"נ אי משום שמחת י"ט קא' הא מת מצוה קודם למגילה כ"ש לשמחת י"ט והאידנ' הכל נקר' מת מצוה ועוד וכי זהו שמחת י"ט לאכול ולילך אח"כ לבית הקברות אין זה אלא תוגה ועוד מאחר דאי' במדרש לא תאכלו על הדם שאין לאכול סעודת קבע קודם שנקבר המת למה נעבור ע"ד המדרש אלא קוברין אותו מיד אחר יציא' בה"כ אם הוא אדם חשוב ואם לאו מתקבצים מנין וקוברין אותו בעת שאו' הש"ץ הפיוטים ושאר דברים כדומה לזה וחוזרים לבה"כ וכן עיקר עכ"ל:
turei_zahav.en: Cover it after eating. Rashel 27:17 and 19, because of the joy of siman 19, is there a dead mitzvah prior to the scroll 29 to the happyness of the 19th and the Eden, everything is cut off, a dead mitzvah, and more, because it is a happy 19th to eat and then go to the cemetery, this is nothing but grief and more, since in the midrash you should not eat on the blood, you should not eat a regular meal before the dead person is buried. In the BHC if he is an important person and if not, they gather from where and bury him when the O'Shetz, the Piyites and other things similar to this and return to the BHC, as well as the main part of Akal:
